ogTitle: Top 10 Popular Attractions in Phuket 2026 — Big Buddha, Old Town, Night Markets
ogDesc: The giant hilltop Buddha, Promthep Cape at sunset, Sino-Portuguese Old Town, Wat Chalong, and lively night markets — 10 Phuket attractions you shouldn't miss, with entry fees and directions.
intro: Phuket isn't only beaches. There's a hilltop giant Buddha with 360-degree views, a pastel Sino-Portuguese Old Town, and weekend night markets bursting with local food. We've rounded up the 10 attractions visitors love most — from the finest sunset viewpoint in Thailand to a walking street overflowing with local bites. Pick your route and head out.

blocks.html:
Mention Phuket and most people picture sand and sea first — but once you actually walk the island, you realise the charm is spread across many different neighbourhoods. Drive up Nakkerd Hill to pay respects to the Big Buddha and take in a 360-degree view of the whole island, then swing south to Promthep Cape to wait out a sea sunset, before looping back into the Old Town to stroll Thalang Road lined with pastel Sino-Portuguese shophouses. Duck into Rommanee Lane for photos, sip coffee inside a century-old building, and by evening there are walking streets and night markets nearly every day of the week. Phuket works beautifully for nature lovers, culture seekers, and shop-and-eat travellers — all in the same trip.

Every spot on this list is one that both locals and visitors consistently call essential to the island. Phra Phuttha Ming Mongkol Eknakakiri — the Big Buddha — is a 45-metre white marble image visible from across Phuket. Wat Chalong (Wat Chaiyathararam) is the island's beloved temple, where devotees come daily to bow before Luang Pho Chaem. Promthep Cape is the legendary sunset point, complete with the Kanchanaphisek Lighthouse. After dark there's Lard Yai Sunday Walking Street, the massive Naka Market, and Bangla Road in Patong for party nights. Line up your days and go.

blocks.name: Phra Phuttha Ming Mongkol Eknakakiri (Big Buddha Phuket)
blocks.area: Karon Sub-district, Mueang Phuket District (Nakkerd Hill summit)
blocks.signature: 45-metre white marble Buddha on a hilltop visible from across the island, with 360-degree views of Kata, Chalong, and Phuket city
blocks.descHtml:
Phra Phuttha Ming Mongkol Eknakakiri — known to everyone simply as Big Buddha Phuket — is a 45-metre white image seated on Nakkerd Hill, roughly 400 metres above sea level. It's the landmark almost no one skips, and it works equally well for those who come to pray, those who come to photograph, and those who just want a quiet viewpoint. The statue is reinforced concrete clad in Burmese white marble weighing over 135 tonnes; in direct sunlight the surface glimmers in a way that photographs simply don't capture. Visitors in reviews consistently say it's larger and more striking in person than it looks online.

The highlight is the 360-degree panorama from the hilltop platform. Looking west you see Kata Beach, Karon, and all the way to Promthep Cape; to the east the view opens over Chalong Bay, the surrounding islands, and the city spread below. On a clear day it's breathtaking. Climb 94 steps to the base of the statue and shoot in every direction. Despite the crowds the atmosphere stays calm and cool. There are bells to ring, birthday-zodiac Buddha images to worship, and a ceramic tile wall where visitors can write a wish.

The budget is easy: free entry, free parking, funded entirely by donations. If you'd like to contribute, do so at your own discretion. Open daily through daylight hours (currently around 09:00–18:00, last entry ~17:30). The golden window is 16:00–17:30 — the light is beautiful and the air cools down. Located in Karon sub-district, the winding road up starts from the Chalong side.

Good to know: this is a sacred site and dress code is enforced at the entrance — no sleeveless tops, no shorts or skirts above the knee. Sarongs are available to borrow for free if needed. Watch your food and belongings around the monkeys. The site reopened in early 2026 after a temporary closure following a landslide; it's worth confirming hours before you go.
mustOrder: 45-metre white marble Buddha image
360-degree view of Kata, Chalong, and Phuket city
Climb 94 steps to the statue's base
Ring the bell and pay respects at birthday-zodiac Buddhas
blocks.bestFor: First-time visitors wanting a 360-degree view in the late afternoon

blocks.name: Promthep Cape
blocks.area: Rawai Sub-district, Mueang Phuket District, Phuket
blocks.signature: One of Thailand's most celebrated sea-sunset viewpoints, with the Kanchanaphisek Lighthouse to climb for elevated panoramas
blocks.descHtml:
Promthep Cape is the southernmost tip of Phuket Island and the sunset viewpoint many people rate the most beautiful in Thailand. It's ideal for couples, families, and photography enthusiasts who want a front-row seat as the sun drops into the Andaman. The cape is a grassy promontory stretching out into the sea, with nearly unobstructed views: the horizon, scattered islets, and vivid emerald water in every direction. First-time visitors to Phuket almost universally have this on their list.

The essential moment is the sunset itself — arrive at least an hour early to secure a good spot and find parking. Up on the headland stands the Kanchanaphisek Lighthouse, built to mark the 50th anniversary of King Rama IX's reign. You can climb up for elevated views and browse the small souvenir shop. Another favourite walk is out to the very tip of the cape, where a path descends to the rocks right at the water's edge. The elephant statue and shrine nearby are popular photo spots too.

The budget is straightforward: free entry, no admission fee. There's a car park, shops, a restaurant, and souvenir stalls where you can sit and rest. Located in Rawai sub-district, about 2 kilometres from Rawai Beach. Open 24 hours, but the sweet spot is 16:30–18:00 when the light is at its peak. Reviews on both Wongnai and international travel sites consistently rate it highly.

One thing to know: the sunset hour draws large crowds, especially in high season and on public holidays. Traffic out can back up after dark and transport home gets tricky. Arrive with time to spare, bring water and a hat because the afternoon sun is strong, and take care on the rocks — the ground can be slippery and the wind picks up at the water's edge.
mustOrder: Watch the sunset from the tip of the cape
Climb the Kanchanaphisek Lighthouse for elevated views
Walk to the very end of the headland for photos
Photo spot at the elephant statue and shrine
blocks.bestFor: Evening sunset watch — great for couples and families
blocks.libCredit: Photo: Promthep Cape · Christophe95 · Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.name: Phuket Old Town (Thalang Road)
blocks.signature: Pastel Sino-Portuguese shophouses filling the entire neighbourhood, Rommanee Lane, cafés, souvenir shops, street art, and great photo opportunities day and night
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to understand Phuket city in a single street, Thalang Road in the Old Town is your answer. It's one of the oldest roads on the island — not even 400 metres long, yet packed with over a hundred Sino-Portuguese shophouses painted in sweet pastels: sky blue, pink, yellow, mint green, stretching as far as the eye can see. It suits those who enjoy a relaxed stroll, café culture, photography, and soaking up the atmosphere of a port town whose heritage blends Chinese, Portuguese, and Malay influences.

The must-see highlight is Rommanee Lane — a narrow alley branching off Thalang Road where vibrant facade colours have made it arguably the most photographed lane in the neighbourhood. Continue through the sois and you'll find street murals tucked into corners: scenes of sea-gypsy life, sparrows, and vignettes from Old Town history. Along the way there are stylish cafés in old buildings, souvenir shops, local pastry stalls, and Hokkien restaurants to stop at whenever you feel like it. Come in the daytime for clean architectural light; return in the evening when warm building lights create a completely different mood.

Walking the area is entirely free — you only spend on coffee, snacks, or whatever catches your eye. The Old Town sits in the centre of Phuket city and connects easily to Dibuk Road, Yaowarat Road, and Krabi Road. Most shops open from mid-morning to evening; the streets themselves are accessible any time. A major draw is the Sunday evening Lard Yai Walking Street, when the road is closed to traffic and the entire stretch becomes a walking market.

People love it because the photos come out well from every angle, day or night. Most reviews praise the classic atmosphere and how enjoyable it is to wander. One practical note: midday sun is intense — bring an umbrella or come in the morning or late afternoon. On Sunday evenings when the walking street runs, the crowds are especially large, so leave extra time and plan parking in advance.
mustOrder: Rommanee Lane pastel shophouses
Street murals hidden in the alleyways
Café inside a Sino-Portuguese building
Lard Yai Sunday Walking Street
blocks.bestFor: Café hoppers and photographers who want a relaxed afternoon stroll

blocks.name: Wat Chalong (Wat Chaiyathararam)
blocks.area: Chalong Sub-district, Mueang Phuket District, Phuket
blocks.signature: Phuket's most beloved temple — the Phra Mahathat Chedi Phra Chom Thai Barami Prakat, and the revered statue of Luang Pho Chaem that devotees come to worship
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to make merit at a temple in Phuket, Wat Chalong — officially Wat Chaiyathararam — is the first name most people put on the list. It's the island's most important community temple, visited constantly by Phuket residents and both Thai and international tourists. The heart of the complex is the statue and likeness of Luang Pho Chaem, a revered monk known for his healing powers, together with Luang Pho Chuang and Luang Pho Kluem — all popular figures for those seeking blessings on health and prosperity. Ideal for those who want to begin a trip with merit-making or are interested in southern Thai temple culture.

The centrepiece is the Phra Mahathat Chedi Phra Chom Thai Barami Prakat — a large golden chedi housing Buddha relics brought from Sri Lanka. You can climb to the upper floors for a view over Phuket's town and surrounding countryside, and each level features intricate Buddhist murals telling the life story of the Buddha. One thing unique to this temple is the firecrackers lit to fulfil vows: the sound reverberates loudly when someone's wish comes true, a sight you rarely see at most temples.

The budget is easy: free entry, no admission fee — just donation boxes if you wish to contribute. Small shops selling offerings, flowers, incense, and snacks line the temple perimeter. Located in Chalong sub-district, not far from the town centre; easy to reach by car or hired transport, with a large car park. Open approximately 07:00–17:00 daily, with the temple grounds accessible all day.

Good to know: dress modestly — shoulders and knees covered, shoes off before entering buildings. The grounds can get hot, so bring an umbrella and water. Most reviews note the temple is kept clean, leafy, and more impressive than expected. On weekends it gets busy; for comfortable exploration and better photos, come before 10:00 or after 15:00 when the light softens and the crowds thin.
mustOrder: Phra Mahathat Chedi Phra Chom Thai Barami Prakat (climb for views from upper floors)
Pay respects and make offerings at the Luang Pho Chaem statue
View the Buddhist mural paintings inside the chedi
Watch firecracker offerings lit to fulfil vows
blocks.bestFor: Opening your trip with temple merit-making; families and sacred-site seekers

blocks.name: Central Phuket Floresta
blocks.signature: Two-building mall — Festival + Floresta — connected by an indoor sky-walk, luxury brand zone, and Aquaria Phuket aquarium
blocks.priceRange: Free to enter · Aquaria from ~THB 540 (book online)
blocks.descHtml:
When Phuket's rain or blazing sun makes outdoor plans unappealing, this is where people retreat for the day. Central Phuket Floresta is the newer luxury wing of Central Phuket, paired with the original Festival building and connected by a covered indoor sky-walk bridging both sides of the road — no stepping outside required. The architecture takes a tropical-forest-meets-Thai-art theme: high ceilings, cool air, open sightlines. Perfect for shoppers, café explorers, and families with children.

The attraction many people come specifically for is Aquaria Phuket on basement level B1 — tens of thousands of aquatic creatures across more than 400 species, with a glass tunnel that lets you walk through while sharks and rays glide overhead. Children love it. The fashion crowd will find the luxury brand zone running from ground floor to first floor — Gucci, Dior, Louis Vuitton, Prada, Hermès, Bvlgari — the most concentrated designer retail on the island. When you need a break there's plenty to eat: the Taste of the Island food court featuring southern Thai and local dishes, Thai restaurants, conveyor-belt sushi, and fine-dining rooms.

Walking the mall is free; parking is available, and the Floresta side has more space and is generally easier to park. For Aquaria, booking online in advance saves a meaningful amount compared to buying on the door — adult tickets start at around THB 540+, children slightly less. Most reviews praise how clean and spacious it is, though weekends bring crowds and the motorcycle park gets tight after 11:00.

Located on Wichit Songkram Road, Wichit sub-district, close to Phuket town — convenient from Patong Beach or the airport. Open daily 10:30–22:00 (Aquaria closes earlier, around 19:00). If Aquaria is the goal, book tickets online beforehand and allow enough time — it's well worth it.
mustOrder: Sky-walk connecting Festival and Floresta buildings
Aquaria Phuket aquarium on level B1
Luxury brand zone Gucci, Dior, Louis Vuitton on floors G–1
Taste of the Island Food Court
blocks.bestFor: Escaping the heat indoors, luxury shopping, taking children to the aquarium

blocks.name: Phuket Walking Street — Lard Yai
blocks.area: Thalang Road, Old Town Quarter, Mueang Phuket District
blocks.signature: Sunday evening walking street in the Old Town heart — local food, handmade goods, live music, all framed by Sino-Portuguese shophouses
blocks.priceRange: Free entry (food and shopping budget from a few hundred THB)
blocks.descHtml:
If you happen to be in Phuket on a Sunday, this is the first place to head. Lard Yai — Phuket Walking Street — is the weekly closure of Thalang Road in the heart of the Old Town, turning the entire length into a pedestrian market. Both sides of the road are lined with pastel Sino-Portuguese buildings lit up with warm evening light. Walking through it feels like stepping back into Phuket a century ago. It's ideal for those who want local food, handmade goods, live music, and Old Town atmosphere all in one evening.

The food is the star. Multiple foreign reviewers describe it as one of the largest and most varied street food markets they've encountered — from southern Thai and local Phuket dishes to Thai classics, desserts, and cold drinks. The craft stalls offer ceramics, portrait paintings, knitted dolls, and an array of handmade items. Scattered through the street are live music stages and busking performers you can stop to watch for free. The energy is genuinely lively.

Free entry, no gate fee. Spend only what you feel like eating or shopping for; most food is inexpensive and a few hundred THB is plenty for a full wander. Open Sundays only, approximately 16:00–22:00, on Thalang Road in the Old Town. It's popular because it packages everything a visitor could want from Phuket Old Town — food, souvenirs, architecture, and authentic community — into a single evening.

One caveat that nearly every review mentions: it gets very crowded after about 19:00, with significant jostling and humidity. For comfortable walking and better photos, arrive around 17:00. Bring cash — many stalls prefer it. Parking nearby is scarce on Sunday evenings; if you're staying in the Old Town, walk over.
mustOrder: Local Phuket and southern Thai street food
Desserts and cold drinks
Handmade crafts, ceramics, and portrait art
Live music and busking performances
blocks.bestFor: Sunday evening food walk in the Old Town

blocks.name: Bangla Road, Patong Beach
blocks.signature: A 400-metre pedestrian nightlife strip packed with bars, clubs, live music, neon lights, and street performances — right across from Patong Beach
blocks.priceRange: Free to walk · drinks from THB 150+
blocks.descHtml:
When Phuket nightlife comes up, no other street matches the sound and spectacle of Bangla Road in Patong. This 400-metre pedestrian strip cuts from Patong Beach Road into the entertainment district. Come evening, vehicles are barred and the street fills with people; both sides are packed with beer bars, clubs, live music, neon signs, and promoters calling from the doorways. If you're after a buzzing night out, this is the obvious starting point.

Bangla's main draw is the experience of simply walking it. Pass open-air bars where live bands play different sets, catch a dance performance or street entertainer at one corner, and stumble into a club at another. Major clubs like Illuzion, Sugar Club, and Tiger sit along the strip, open until dawn with DJ sets running all night. The peak energy is roughly 21:00 to 01:00 when the lights are blazing and music comes from every direction. Those who prefer something quieter can find bars with softer live music or a pool table where you can sip a cold beer and watch the passing crowd.

The street itself is free to walk. Reviews put drinks at around THB 150 and up; some larger clubs charge entry of roughly THB 300–500 depending on the night, sometimes including one drink. Located directly opposite Patong Beach — a short walk from the shore. Open every night but genuinely comes alive after sunset.

Tips from real reviews: always ask for prices before ordering, especially for seafood like grilled lobster where unexpected bills have caught people out. Be cautious with roadside games that invite you to play for money, and keep your wallet and valuables secure in the thick crowds. It's popular precisely because it is Phuket's true centre of nighttime entertainment. One visit makes it clear why everyone talks about it.
mustOrder: Walk the entire 400-metre pedestrian strip
Live music at open-air bars
Major clubs — Illuzion / Sugar Club / Tiger
Neon lights and street performers
blocks.libCredit: Photo: Bangla Road, Patong · Karelj · Wikimedia Commons · Public Domain

blocks.name: Suan Chalerm Phra Kiat (Rama IX Public Park)
blocks.signature: Phuket's largest public park — about 350 rai — with a running track, cycling lane, a central lake, outdoor gym equipment, and dinosaur statues for children to photograph
blocks.descHtml:
If you want to know where Phuket residents go to exercise and relax with their families, the answer is Suan Chalerm Phra Kiat — or as everyone calls it, the Rama IX Public Park. It's the largest public park in Phuket city, covering about 350 rai on land that was once a tin mine, now transformed into a green lung in the city centre with abundant trees, shade, and a large central lake. It suits walkers and joggers, cyclists, outdoor fitness enthusiasts, and families with children who want room to run.

The highlights include a proper running loop around the park, a dedicated cycling lane, and outdoor gym equipment dotted on both sides of the path. What children love most are the large dinosaur statues scattered around the park — they've become the go-to photo spots. There are also playgrounds, a basketball court, a badminton court, and an aerobics plaza where groups gather for morning and evening sessions. In the late afternoon the view of the sunset reflected on the lake draws people to sit and enjoy the breeze.

The budget is excellent: free entry, no admission fee, free parking. Food vendors and fresh fruit stalls line the paths. Located on Phatthana Road, Soi 14, Mueang Phuket District — close to the city centre and the night markets. Open every day from early morning to evening. Most locals come in the early morning before the heat builds, or in the late afternoon after work.

It's popular because it's a well-maintained green space that's accessible, genuinely large, and works for all purposes — exercise, picnics, bringing children, or simply sitting quietly. One practical note: midday sun is strong and the park is expansive. If you're walking far, bring water and a hat. For the full community atmosphere, visit in the morning or evening when the park fills with locals living their daily lives.
mustOrder: Dinosaur statues — the park's go-to photo spots
Running track and cycling lane around the park
Central lake with sunset views
Morning and evening aerobics sessions
blocks.bestFor: Morning or evening exercise; family outings

blocks.name: Phuket Weekend Night Market (Naka Market)
blocks.signature: Phuket's largest weekend night market — hundreds of stalls, clearly divided into a food zone and a shopping zone, with a grilled seafood section and live music
blocks.descHtml:
The Phuket Weekend Night Market — widely known as Naka Market (formerly Naka Trunk Market / Chaofa Variety Market) — is the largest weekend night market on the island. It started over ten years ago as a small second-hand swap meet, and has grown into a multi-hundred-stall spread divided clearly into a food zone and a shopping zone. Great for anyone who wants a relaxed, affordable evening meal, a long browse, or a fun outing with a group or family.

The highlight most reviewers mention is the grilled seafood zone — prawns, fish, and fresh seafood that many say is noticeably cheaper than at other markets. Beyond that there's a full street-food lineup: mango sticky rice, banana roti, takoyaki, fresh fruit juices, and even fried insects for the adventurous. The shopping zone covers clothing, elephant pants (around THB 150–200), souvenirs, bags, shoes, and phone accessories. The atmosphere is lively with live music and shared tables where people eat together — the kind of place that feels genuinely local rather than staged for tourists.

Free entry, no gate fee. Budget roughly THB 200–500 per person for a comfortable browse, eat, and shop. Open Saturdays and Sundays only, evenings from about 16:00–22:00. Located on Wirapon Hongyok Road (west Chaofa), near Central Phuket, on the suburban side of the city — about 3 kilometres from the Old Town. Parking is available but fills up during peak hours; many people prefer to arrive by taxi or tuk-tuk.

It's popular because it genuinely has everything in one place: satisfying food, good shopping, a covered roof for sun and rain, and the feel of a real local market — not a tourist showcase. Key tip: it only opens on weekends. Arrive during a weekday and you'll find it closed. Coming at the start of the evening avoids the peak crowd rush.
mustOrder: Grilled seafood — prawns and fish
Mango sticky rice
Banana roti
Elephant pants / souvenirs
blocks.bestFor: Weekend evening dinner — eat, browse, and hang out as a group
blocks.spice: Options ranging from mild to spicy

blocks.name: Lard Ploi Khong (Phuket Indy Market)
blocks.area: Limelight Avenue, Dibuk Road, Talat Yai Sub-district, Mueang Phuket District
blocks.signature: Indie night market in the city centre — clothing, handmade goods, jewellery, a food zone at the back, and live music from student performers
blocks.descHtml:
Lard Ploi Khong (Phuket Indy Market) is a small indie night market in central Phuket city, started from the simple idea of letting young creatives set up stalls in the lane next to Limelight Avenue on Dibuk Road — a short walk from Thalang Road in the Old Town. It's perfect for anyone who wants a relaxed evening wander without the push of a big market, or is looking for handmade goods, vintage and new youth-fashion pieces, or a light bite before dinner.

The layout is designed so you can see it all in a single pass: stalls of souvenirs and jewellery at the entrance, clothing, shoes, and bags in the middle, then the food zone at the back — which is the real star. Reviews consistently describe the food as fresh, tasty, and reasonably priced, averaging around THB 30–60 per dish. Expect spring rolls, Pad Thai, sushi, fried chicken, grilled pork skewers, and mango sticky rice. The thing not to miss is sitting with a plate while a small stage nearby hosts live performances — often schoolchildren showing off their talents. The atmosphere is warm and neighbourly.

Free entry. A few hundred THB covers a comfortable browse and meal. Open Wednesdays, Thursdays, and Fridays only, approximately 16:00–22:30. Reviewers appreciate that it's small, clean, and quick to explore — 15–20 minutes gets you through the whole thing. The location next to Limelight mall is handy: if the heat gets to you, walk straight into the air-conditioned shopping centre.

It's popular because it's one of Phuket's original indie markets and gives you the feeling of real city life rather than a tourist showcase. Note that it's smaller than other well-known markets and variety is more limited. Come in the evening when all stalls are open and the live music is running, then extend the night with a stroll through the Old Town nearby.
mustOrder: Back food zone: Pad Thai, sushi, grilled pork, fried chicken
Mango sticky rice
Fresh spring rolls
Live music from the small stage
blocks.bestFor: Relaxed evening out + indie market browse in the Old Town

items.title: Getting around
items.text: Attractions are spread across multiple districts. A rental car or Grab is the most convenient option. Phuket taxis and tuk-tuks are expensive and rarely use meters — always agree on the price before you get in.

items.title: Carry cash
items.text: Most stalls at night markets and walking streets accept cash only. Keep small notes handy. Some stalls are introducing QR Pay, but it's not universal. Large malls and restaurants accept cards as normal.

items.title: Avoid the midday heat and queues
items.text: Visit Big Buddha and Wat Chalong in the morning when the sun is milder and crowds are smaller. For Promthep Cape, arrive at least an hour before sunset to secure a spot and find parking.

items.title: Dress for temples
items.text: Big Buddha and Wat Chalong are sacred sites. Cover shoulders and knees. Sarongs are available to borrow for free at Big Buddha if you're not dressed appropriately.

items.title: Language and signage
items.text: Major attractions and malls have English signage and staff who can communicate in English. Local markets may be Thai-only, but pointing at pictures or using a translation app makes ordering food easy.

items.title: Tipping
items.text: Restaurants and cafés in the city don't require a tip, though a small gesture for good service is appreciated. Guides and tour drivers customarily receive a small tip at the end of the trip.

blocks.title: Plan a well-paced Phuket day in one route
blocks.html: The most efficient route is to start in the morning at Big Buddha on Nakkerd Hill while the air is cool and the site is quiet, then stop at Wat Chalong nearby on the way down. Drive south to Promthep Cape in the mid to late afternoon to claim a good spot before the sunset crowd arrives. Once the sun drops, loop back into Phuket Old Town for an evening on Thalang Road — if it's Sunday, Lard Yai Walking Street will be in full swing. On Saturday or Sunday evenings Naka Market is open; on Thursday and Friday evenings Lard Ploi Khong (Phuket Indy Market) runs in the Old Town. Match your days to the market you want and the trip packs itself. Anyone wanting air-conditioned relief during the day can slot in Central Phuket Floresta and Aquaria Phuket. Party nights belong to Bangla Road in Patong.

blocks.text: Covering Phuket's highlights is much smoother with a well-placed base. Stay in the Old Town to walk to the night markets and cafés, or stay near Patong or Kata for the beach and Bangla Road. Book in advance during high season for the best rates.

faq.q: What are the must-see attractions in Phuket?
faq.a: For a first visit, the essential three are Phra Phuttha Ming Mongkol Eknakakiri (Big Buddha) on Nakkerd Hill for panoramic views, Promthep Cape for the sea sunset, and Phuket Old Town on Thalang Road for its Sino-Portuguese shophouses. Add Wat Chalong (Wat Chaiyathararam) as the island's most important temple. These four consistently top visitor lists.

faq.q: What makes Phuket unique compared to other Thai destinations?
faq.a: Phuket's Old Town neighbourhood with its pastel Sino-Portuguese shophouses — especially Thalang Road and Rommanee Lane — is something you won't find anywhere else. Add the 360-degree panorama from Big Buddha where you see Kata Beach, Chalong Bay, and Phuket city in one glance, and the sea sunset at Promthep Cape which many consider the finest in Thailand.

faq.q: Do Phuket's attractions charge an entry fee?
faq.a: Most are free: Big Buddha (donations welcome), Promthep Cape, Wat Chalong, the Old Town, Rama IX Public Park, and the various night markets all have free entry. The main paid attraction is Aquaria Phuket inside Central Phuket Floresta, starting at around THB 540 when booked online. Bangla Road is free to walk; drinks inside bars start from about THB 150.

faq.q: How do I get around Phuket and where do I park?
faq.a: Attractions are spread across several districts — a rental car or Grab is the most convenient way to move between them. Big Buddha, Promthep Cape, Wat Chalong, and Rama IX Public Park all have their own car parks. For Phuket Old Town and the Lard Yai Walking Street, park nearby and walk in, as the road closes on Sunday evenings and traffic is heavy. Bangla Road in Patong is pedestrianised — park in the surrounding streets and walk in.

faq.q: What are the opening hours of Phuket's night venues?
faq.a: Lard Yai Walking Street runs Sunday evenings only. Naka Market is open Saturday and Sunday evenings. Lard Ploi Khong (Phuket Indy Market) opens Thursday and Friday evenings. Bangla Road in Patong is lively every night from early evening onward. Check the schedule before planning so your evening lines up with the market you want.
